claims.text: A production possibility curve (PPC) is a boundary showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce in a given period when its resources are employed fully and efficiently.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A PPC is drawn for a given state of resources and technology, so the stock of resources and the know-how worked into them are held unchanged for the period the curve covers.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A PPC slopes downward from left to right because producing more of one good requires withdrawing resources from the other good, so the quantity of the second good falls.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A PPC tends to bow outward because resources are not equally suited to the two goods, so the sacrifice of the good given up tends to grow as more of the other good is produced.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A point on a PPC shows resources fully and efficiently employed; a point under it shows resources idle or misused, so output could be higher; a point beyond it shows an output the current boundary cannot reach.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An economy producing inside its PPC can raise the output of one or both goods without sacrificing the other, because idle or misused resources can be brought into use.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A point beyond a PPC may become reachable if the boundary shifts outward through growth of the economy productive capacity.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A movement along a PPC is a reallocation of resources between the two goods while the economy remains on the boundary, with the boundary itself unchanged.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Each movement along a PPC carries an opportunity cost, the quantity of the good given up for the quantity gained, and that cost tends to rise as the movement continues.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A movement along a PPC changes the combination of goods chosen while capacity is unchanged, whereas a shift of a PPC changes the capacity itself.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A movement along a PPC and a shift of a PPC are told apart by what happened to the maximum possible output: an unchanged maximum means a movement along the curve, and a changed maximum means a shift of it.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A shift of a PPC outward shows growth of the economy productive capacity, so more of at least one good can be produced than before; an inward shift shows capacity shrinking.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: An outward shift of a PPC tends to follow from more resources, better-trained workers or improved technology, and an inward shift tends to follow from destruction of resources.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A point that lay beyond an old PPC may sit on or inside the new boundary after an outward shift, because the boundary moved rather than the chosen point sliding along it.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The consequences of a shift of a PPC land on consumers, whose obtainable output changes, and on workers, whose employment depends on the capacity the boundary describes.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
